label: text
text: The miners' leaders were hurriedly summoned from Bournemouth and conferred for two hours with the Coal Committee of the Cabinet. Downing Street till after midnight.

label: text

Mr. A. J. Cook, on being interviewed today before returning to Bournemouth, refused to disclose the nature of the conversation, but it is believed that the Government, supported by public opinion, will bring the coal owners to meet the miners in a three-party conference to negotiate a national settlement.
A letter of to-day's date which Mr. Winston Churchill addressed to Mr. Evan Williams, President of the Mining Association, and issued to-night, explains in detail the kind of three-party conference which the Government contemplates. It says that such a conference could only

label: paragraph_title
text: UNIQUE TRIAL

label: paragraph_title
text: EX-ATTORNEY-GENERAL CHARGED.

label: text
text: ALLEGED BRIBES.

label: text
text:
The trial of Henry Daugherty and Thomas Miller, which has been opened here, is unique inasmuch as it is the first recorded under the Federal Criminal Law of a member of the Cabinet for alleged misdeeds during his term of office.
Judge Mack is presiding at the trial: Mr. Max Stever, reputed to be one of the shrewdest New York lawyers, is leading the defence.

label: text
text: "It is claimed that Daugherty, and Miller and other accused received large fees for their part in authorizing the return of the so-called American Metals Company" to its European owners after the war. It is alleged that these sums were furnished by Henry Richard Nerton, of Frankfurt-on-Main, President of the German Corporation which originally owned the metal concern.

label: text
text: The United States Attorney, Mr. Bancory Buckner, is conducting the Government brief.

label: text
text: The Government contends that approximately $400,000 was paid in bribes whereupon Miller, with the approval of Daugherty, turned over to the European claimants the $7,000,000 realised from the sale of the Metals Company.

label: text
text:
Herr Morton, who is the Government's star witness, in his evidence gave dates of his visits to the United States and his meetings with an alleged intermediary named King (who is now dead) and others.
The hearing has been adjourned.
—Reuter's American Service.

label: text

Mr.�.z, replying in the Assembly to-day to Mr. Venkatapatiraj's question regarding an opportunity for the Assembly to discuss the proposals regarding minimum wages for Indian labourers in Ceylon, and Malaya said that the proposals regarding the fixation of standard minimum wages for the Indian estate labourer in Ceylon and British Malaya had been made after full consultation with the Standing Committee on Emigration. Any agreement on most questions had been reached with the Government of Ceylon, and the Government of India hoped to issue a communiqué reviewing the points of settlement as soon as negotiations on certain minor points, which were still under discussion, were completed.

label: paragraph_title
text: WEIRD DOCTORING

label: text
text: A party of distinguished medical men has just visited Horton Mental Hospital, Epsom, to see the manner in which the malaria-carrying mosquito is used to cure general paralysis. In 1917 German investigators discovered that the bite of the anopheline mosquito was an effective remedy for general paralysis. In British mental hospitals the treatment has proved so successful that world-wide interest is now being taken in it. Before being employed as "prescriptions," the insects infect themselves with the malaria germ. They are then made to bite patients, suffering from general paralysis, and when malaria is thus set up it has the effect of "killing" the paralysis. Quinine is then given the patient to free him from malaria. Weird though this form of doctoring may seem, it gives a high percentage of successes, and is the only known process by which general paralysis can be combated effectively.

text: POWDER ON POTATOES

label: text
text: The spectacle of an aeropla showering down powder from the air on a 45-acres field of potatoes to protect them from diseases excited great interest among South Lincolnshire agriculturists.

label: text
text: Mr. George Caudwell, of Weston, near Spalding, one of the largest growers of potatoes in the British Isles, chartered a private aeroplane, piloted by Major Savage, to experiment on a field of “Majesties.”

label: text
text: The powder was contained in two pipes on either side of the fuselage, and the machine worked first down and then across the field, being so low that at times the wheels appeared nearly to touch the tops of the potatoes.

label: text

GAME HUNTING THRILLS IN
KOMODO.

label: text
text: Some of the biggest big-game hunting thrills ever experienced should be forthcoming shortly, up in the mountains of one of the islands of the Dutch East Indies, where efforts are to be made to trap the last great uncaptured wild beast in the world, a fierce man-eating lizard, 30 ft. long when full grown, which may have been the original dragon that has pervaded Chinese mythology with dragon-lore.

label: text
text:

The place where this great lizard survives is the island of Komodo, in the Sunda Sen, between Flores and Sumbawa, some 00 miles south-east of Borneo. The last time I was out in the Malay Archipelago, writes an ex-forer to the "Manchester Guardian," I managed to obtain, from various Dutch colonial officials' idings of some personal experiences with the creature. Only little ones have hitherto been killed, or the simple reason that the big ones, which have several times seen sighted, go killing on their own account with such zest that it is very difficult to induce natives to accompany a white man after them. They can move as fast as motor-car, and they are quite earless in going to the defence of their young. Their tough, scaly side is impervious to native weapons, and even with a high velocity rifle it is hard to get a hot that will stop their onrush.
Lieutenant J. K. H. van Steyr van Hensbroek, when Civil Administrator of the coastal settlement at Reo, on Flores, crossed to Comodo, investigated the rumours which had reached him, shot young "dragon". 7 ft. long, and reserved the skin. He was unable to obtain one of the big ones to found the natives very reluctant to participate in his hunting they called the monster the Boeadasat, or Crocodile of the Land it is no crocodile, however, for examination of several skins have shown clearly that it is a giant member of the Varanus family of lizards. It has a short snout and sharp teeth. A kind of raised steel runs down the middle of the back, rising, at the tail, into five-peaked crest somewhat resembling that "of our own little pond newt. It slashes right and left with this tail when angry. I has a yellow tongue, nearly a yard ong, which, on occasion, it dart in and out of its mouth. (The Chinese dragon, you will recollect as portrayed with a long yellowish or reddish tongue, or yellowish or reddish flame darting from its open jaws.) An amazing thing about it is that it is deaf, though not "stone" deaf. But its neck is so limber that its constantly wisting and turning head makes the task of approaching it un

label: text
text: After Lieutenant van Steyn van Hensbroek's visit, a local chief, the Rajah Bitjara, accompanied by a native collector sent out by the Dutch Museum at Buitenzorg, in Java, bagged four young ones, 9 ft., 7½ ft., and 3 ft. (two) respectively. Sergeant Beker, of the Dutch Colonial Army, bagged a 13-footer, but was unable to shoot one of the big fellows, as he found the risk too great to be tackled single-handed. Herr Aldegon, another Dutchman, shot some young.

label: text
text: Like robber barons of old, the “dragons” live up aloft on bare hills, where they can see every moving creature long before it can reach them. Their sleeping quarters are in bamboo thickets around springs at the head of rocky gullies. Here they spend the night in lairs hollowed out under overhanging rocks, awakening at dawn to prowl for their prey. The risks of tackling them can be appreciated when it is mentioned that they sometimes go about in parties of a dozen or more, that there are no trees to climb, and that, raising themselves on their hind legs, the adults could quite easily make a mouthful of a man as high up a rock or pole as the top of a motorbus. Aldegon “ground-baited” for them with carcases of wild boar.

label: text
text: The only prudent way of going after the big ones would be in an armoured car or a tank. The two expeditions are not to be envied the job of mollifying one (or more) sufficiently to induce it to emigrate, alive, to the United States!

label: paragraph_title

label: text
text: YACHT "ST. GEORGE."

label: text
text: The story of the financial difficulties of a scientific expedition to the South Pacific undertaken by a party of experts in the steam yacht "St. George" in October 1924 was told in the Admiralty Court, London.

label: text
text: The matter came before the Court at the instance of Major Archibald Douglas, a director of the Company, who organised the expedition, and Mr. William Alexander Grant, of Hillersdon, Cullompton, Devon, one of the passengers on the yacht.

label: text
text: The former claimed £200 and the later £1,000, advanced to assist the expedition when the yacht had got through the Panama Canal and was stranded for lack of funds.

label: text
text: Mr. Balloch for the plaintiffs, said a company called Research Expedition (Ltd.), with a capital of £3,000, was formed to own the yacht. The vessel cost £8,350 and a further £16,815 was spent in fitting her for the voyage. To meet these liabilities Mr. Gates advanced £25,000 on mortgage. The mortgagee had already obtained judgment on his mortgage and the vessel had been sold by order of the Court, realising £6,600.

label: text
text: Major Douglas said the expedition achieved most interesting results. They had hoped to repay advances by means of a film of the trip, which unfortunately did not pay.

label: text
text: Mr. Grant said that he, like the six other passengers who accompanied the expedition, paid £700 for the trip. He advanced the loans to enable the ship to get on. They were held up at one point for such a long time for lack of funds that he could not stand it any longer. After a long legal argument as to the validity of the bottomry bounds the President reserved judgment.
